content: 1. During the reporting period, individuals who started antiretroviral therapy (ART) are recorded, along with disaggregated data by sex and age groups (<15 years and 15+ years). 2. Tuberculosis (TB) preventive therapy using isoniazid is a critical component of the World Health Organization (WHO) TB/HIV Three I’s strategy. It is an essential part of comprehensive HIV care to prevent TB in people living with HIV. 3. WHO strongly recommends a minimum six-month course of TB preventive therapy for all people living with HIV, excluding those with presumed or confirmed active TB. For individuals in high TB transmission settings, a conditional recommendation is made for a minimum 36-month course of TB preventive therapy. 4. The indicator for ART initiation has been revised to reflect started on ART instead of newly enrolled in HIV care, aligning with the treat all recommendations. 5. In countries with less than 90% ART coverage among those enrolled in HIV care, patients not yet started on ART (and without active TB) may be included in the denominator. Patients who began TB preventive therapy at the time of enrollment in care are added to the numerator. 6. Hepatitis C screening involves testing for HBsAg and HCV antibodies, followed by HCV RNA testing for those who are anti-HCV positive. Newly added columns in the ART register are used to track these indicators. 7. The numerator and denominator definitions for ART initiation have been revised to reflect newly initiated on ART instead of in HIV care, consistent with the treat all guidelines. 8. The on-time pill pick-up indicator measures the percentage of ART patients who collect all prescribed antiretroviral (ARV) drugs on or before the pill run-out date. This indicator assesses clinic-level performance in ensuring timely medication adherence. 9. WHO recommends a target of over 90% for on-time pill pick-up as excellent performance, 80–90% as fair, and less than 80% as poor. Sustained adherence to ART is critical for achieving individual and population-level benefits of HIV treatment. 10. Studies show that treatment interruptions of more than 48 hours in individuals on non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NNRTI)-based regimens can lead to virological failure and the development of drug-resistant HIV. 11. Although the risk of HIV drug resistance (HIVDR) is lower with non-NNRTI-based regimens, maximizing population-level viral load suppression is essential to achieving the third 90 target. 12. Estimating ART adherence can be challenging due to the unreliability of self-reported adherence and provider perceptions. Pharmacy records are generally more accurate for tracking on-time pill pick-up. 13. On-time pill pick-up has been observed to predict clinic-level viral load suppression. Identifying clinics with suboptimal pill pick-up rates and targeting their patient populations for adherence interventions may improve overall viral load suppression and health outcomes. 14. Linking pharmacy visits to clinical records is crucial to harmonize patient data and facilitate interventions like loss-to-follow-up tracing and adherence counseling. 15. ART-related toxicities are a common reason for poor adherence, treatment discontinuation, or drug substitution. Monitoring these toxicities provides data on their incidence, clinical significance, and impact on patient outcomes. 16. A new indicator for treatment-limiting toxicity has been introduced in the WHO 2015 consolidated guidelines for national program monitoring. 17. The numerator for this indicator includes the number of people living with HIV on ART who substituted a regimen or interrupted treatment due to toxicity within the past 12 months. 18. The denominator includes all patients on ART during the reporting period. Data sources include HIV patient cards and ART registers. 19. Viral suppression is a cohort-based indicator measuring the proportion of patients on ART for 12 months who achieve viral load suppression (<1000 copies/mL). 20. WHO recommends a target of 90% or greater viral load suppression for desirable clinic performance, 80–90% as fair, and less than 80% as poor. 21. Viral load suppression at 12 months is a reliable early indicator of treatment success and can be collected using routine patient monitoring systems. 22. Pregnant and breastfeeding women may require more frequent viral load monitoring to prevent HIV transmission. Newly initiated pregnant women on ART need close follow-up, and 3-month viral load suppression may serve as a useful marker for adherence issues. 23. In the general population, 6-month viral load suppression can help address early adherence issues among patients newly started on ART. 24. Health workers can use ART registers to scan patient cohorts for 6-month viral load results and follow up with patients with viral loads above 1000 copies/mL. 25. Achieving high levels of viral load suppression minimizes morbidity, mortality, and HIV incidence while preventing the emergence of HIV drug resistance. 26. Co-trimoxazole (CTX) prophylaxis is an integral component of HIV care to prevent common coinfections. WHO recommends CTX for all HIV-positive adults and children in settings with high malaria or severe bacterial infections, all HIV-positive children under 5 years, and adults with advanced HIV disease or CD4 counts <200 cells/mm³. 27. The CTX coverage indicator measures the percentage of eligible HIV-positive individuals receiving CTX prophylaxis. Data is collected through annual reviews of HIV patient cards or ART registers. 28. The numerator includes the number of eligible HIV-positive individuals who received CTX, while the denominator includes all eligible individuals enrolled in HIV care. 29. Viral load testing coverage measures the proportion of patients with a 12-month viral load test result in their medical records. WHO recommends a target of ≥70% for this indicator. 30. Routine viral load monitoring and appropriate action to address virological failure are essential to prevent the emergence of HIV drug resistance.
